meta.name: AGCF — Agentic Governance & Control Framework
meta.summary: A vendor-neutral reference architecture and self-assessment instrument for governing AI agents, assistants and automation. Scales from an individual practitioner to a regulated enterprise.

planes.name: Foundation
planes.desc: Who is accountable, and what do we actually have running.

planes.name: Trust Gate
planes.desc: What may enter, on whose authority, under what policy. Evaluated before the agent reasons or acts.

planes.name: Execution
planes.desc: What the agent may do, how far the damage can travel, who can stop it, and what is recorded.

planes.name: Assurance & Learning
planes.desc: How we know it works, what happens when it doesn't, and how the system improves.

tiers.name: Individual / Solo
tiers.desc: One person or a handful, no dedicated security or compliance function. Personal or small-client work. The bar is: know what you're running, don't leak, don't let it break things you can't undo.

tiers.name: Small–Mid Organization
tiers.desc: Has IT, may have security. Real customer or employee data. Contractual and sectoral obligations. The bar is: repeatable process, technical enforcement, evidence you can produce on request.

tiers.name: Enterprise / Regulated
tiers.desc: Formal risk function, audit, regulator or large-customer scrutiny. The bar is: policy as code, independent assurance, evidence that survives adversarial review.

autonomy.name: Advisory
autonomy.desc: Reads and answers. No access to systems of record, no actions. A chat assistant with no tools.

autonomy.name: Assistive
autonomy.desc: Reads organizational data and produces artifacts a human then uses. Retrieval, summarization, drafting. Reads real data; writes nothing.

autonomy.name: Gated executor
autonomy.desc: Proposes actions in real systems; a human approves each consequential one before it happens.

autonomy.name: Bounded autonomous
autonomy.desc: Executes within a pre-approved envelope without per-action approval. Humans supervise on the loop, not in it.

autonomy.name: Open autonomous / multi-agent
autonomy.desc: Sets its own sub-goals, spawns or directs other agents, or operates with an envelope broad enough that its actions cannot be individually anticipated.

status_scale.label: In Place
status_scale.desc: Implemented, operating, and you could show evidence today.

status_scale.label: Partial
status_scale.desc: Exists but incomplete, inconsistent, or unevidenced.

status_scale.label: Must Implement
status_scale.desc: Required at your tier and autonomy level. Absent. Known solution exists — this is execution work.

status_scale.label: Develop
status_scale.desc: Required, absent, and there is no off-the-shelf answer for your context. This is design work, not procurement.

status_scale.label: Not Applicable
status_scale.desc: Genuinely out of scope. Requires a written justification to count.

meta.verification: Crosswalk independently verified 28 Jul 2026 against NIST AI 100-1 Appendix A, ISO/IEC 42001:2023 Annex A, the consolidated AI Act as amended by Reg. (EU) 2026/1744, and OWASP/MCP primary sources. 28 citations corrected.

domains.name: Governance & Accountability
domains.purpose: Someone owns this. There is a written rule about what AI may and may not be used for, people know it, and the rule is reviewed as the ground shifts.
domains.why: Every downstream control inherits its authority from here. Without a named owner and a written boundary, the rest of the framework is a wish list.

controls.title: Named accountable owner
controls.statement: One named person owns AI and agent use and has the authority to stop it. A committee does not satisfy this control.
controls.evidence: Role description, org chart entry, or a line in the AI policy naming the person.

controls.title: Written AI use policy
controls.statement: You have a written policy that states which AI use you permit, which you prohibit, which needs approval, and who decides.
controls.evidence: The policy document, with a version and date. Evidence it was distributed.

controls.title: Risk appetite and prohibited-use list
controls.statement: You have decided, in writing, which categories of AI use you refuse and how much residual risk you accept.
controls.evidence: Prohibited-use list; documented risk tolerance statement approved at the right level.

controls.title: AI literacy and role-based training
controls.statement: You train everyone who builds, operates, or approves an AI system, and everyone the system affects. Training matches the role and covers known failure modes.
controls.evidence: Training materials, completion records, role-to-training mapping.

xw.EU AI Act: Art. 4 (in force since 2 Feb 2025; amended 27 Jul 2026 to a support-and-provide standard)

controls.title: Executive and board accountability
controls.statement: Leadership formally owns AI risk decisions. Leadership reviews those decisions on a defined cadence with primary data, not a status slide.
controls.evidence: Meeting minutes, standing agenda item, escalation records.

controls.title: Cross-functional review body
controls.statement: A standing group with legal, security, privacy, and domain members reviews each new agent use case before it goes live.
controls.evidence: Terms of reference, membership, review records with decisions.

controls.title: Resourcing
controls.statement: You allocate budget and staff time to AI governance as named line items. Governance work belongs to a person, not to spare time.
controls.evidence: Budget line, headcount allocation, or documented time allocation.

controls.title: Contractual flow-down to suppliers
controls.statement: Your supplier contracts contain the AI governance requirements: data use, training rights, incident notice, model change notice, and evidence access.
controls.evidence: Contract clauses, vendor questionnaire, procurement standard.

xw.Other: US: OMB M-25-22 flow-downs for federal contractors

controls.title: Regulatory applicability determination
controls.statement: You know which AI laws apply to you, in which jurisdictions, on which dates. You refresh this determination when the law moves.
controls.evidence: Applicability memo with jurisdictions, obligations and dates; review date.

xw.Other: US state law: CO ADMTA (1 Jan 2027), TX TRAIGA, CA SB 53, IL SB 315

domains.name: AI Register, Classification & Risk Tiering
domains.purpose: You know every AI system and agent operating on your behalf, what each one touches, how autonomous it is, and how much damage it could do.
domains.why: You cannot govern what you cannot enumerate. Inventory is the single highest-leverage control in the framework and the one most often skipped because it is unglamorous.

controls.title: Register of AI systems and agents
controls.statement: You maintain an AI register that lists every AI system and agent in use. The register includes AI features embedded inside SaaS products.
controls.evidence: The register itself, with a last-reviewed date.

controls.title: Register content is sufficient to govern
controls.statement: Each register entry records purpose, business owner, model and provider, reachable data, available tools and actions, and runtime location.
controls.evidence: Register schema and a populated sample.

controls.title: Autonomy tier assigned
controls.statement: You assign each agent an autonomy level, from advisory to open autonomous. The assigned level selects which controls apply.
controls.evidence: Autonomy tier recorded per entry; tier definitions documented.

xw.EU AI Act: Art. 14(1) (oversight proportionate to autonomy); Annex XIII(e)

controls.title: Impact and consequence classification
controls.statement: Each use case records who the outputs affect and how badly, including people who are not your users.
controls.evidence: Impact assessment per use case; affected-population analysis.

controls.title: Regulatory classification per use case
controls.statement: You classify each use case against the applicable regimes: prohibited, high risk, transparency only, or minimal. You record the reasoning.
controls.evidence: Classification record with rationale, reviewed by someone competent to review it.

xw.EU AI Act: Art. 5, Art. 6, Art. 6(3)–(4), Annex III, Art. 50

controls.title: Shadow AI discovery
controls.statement: You operate an active mechanism that finds AI and agent use which skipped the approval process. A policy alone does not satisfy this control.
controls.evidence: Discovery method (egress logs, SaaS discovery, expense review, survey) and findings from the last cycle.

controls.title: Reclassification triggers
controls.statement: Defined events force a new review: model version change, new tool or connector, scope expansion, or a new data domain. Old approvals do not carry over.
controls.evidence: Trigger list; examples of triggered re-reviews.

controls.title: Register reconciled to identity and spend
controls.statement: You reconcile the AI register against issued credentials, connector grants, and billing at least monthly. Undeclared agents appear in those three places.
controls.evidence: Reconciliation report; discrepancies and their resolution.

domains.name: Data Boundary, Provenance & Sovereignty
domains.purpose: The agent can reach exactly the data it needs, that data's origin and handling terms are known, and it does not cross borders or contracts it shouldn't.
domains.why: This is the control most organizations think they have because they have a data classification policy. Having a policy and enforcing it at agent retrieval time are different things.

controls.title: Classification applied to agent-reachable data
controls.statement: You classify every data source an agent can reach. You treat unclassified data as sensitive by default, not as public.
controls.evidence: Classification scheme; classification applied to the sources in the register.

controls.title: Default-deny data scope per agent
controls.statement: Each agent has an explicit allow-list of data domains. Access is default-deny, not everything the service account can see.
controls.evidence: Per-agent scope configuration; a test showing an out-of-scope source is inaccessible.

controls.title: Retrieval-time minimization
controls.statement: The agent receives the least data that completes the task. You filter at retrieval, not in the prompt, and you do not trust the model to filter.
controls.evidence: Retrieval filter configuration; sample trace showing the data actually passed.

controls.title: Sensitive-data detection on both directions
controls.statement: Detection for personal, health, payment, credential, and proprietary data runs on content that enters the agent and on content that leaves it.
controls.evidence: Detector configuration and coverage; recent detection statistics including false-negative testing.

controls.title: De-identification and redaction
controls.statement: Where a task does not need identified data, the agent receives de-identified, redacted, or masked data.
controls.evidence: De-identification method and its validation; documented decision where full fidelity is required.

xw.EU AI Act: Art. 4a (special-category data for bias detection; Art. 10(5) deleted by Reg. (EU) 2026/1744)

controls.title: Residency and sovereignty enforced technically
controls.statement: Configuration and network controls enforce data residency, cross-border transfer limits, and sovereign-compute constraints. A contract clause alone does not satisfy this control.
controls.evidence: Region pinning configuration; egress controls; transfer mechanism documentation.

xw.Other: GDPR Ch. V; sector sovereignty requirements

controls.title: Provider training and retention terms verified
controls.statement: You know, in writing, whether your prompts and data train each provider model, the retention period, and who can access them. This covers every provider, including AI inside your SaaS tools.
controls.evidence: Provider terms extract per provider; configuration proving the elected setting.

controls.title: Provenance for corpora and memory
controls.statement: For each item in a corpus, fine-tuning set, or agent memory, you can name its origin, its writer, and its write time.
controls.evidence: Provenance metadata schema; sample lineage trace.

controls.title: Retention and deletion across the whole footprint
controls.statement: Retention and deletion rules cover prompts, outputs, embeddings, agent memory, and execution traces. The rules do not stop at the system of record.
controls.evidence: Retention schedule naming each store; evidence of deletion executing.

xw.EU AI Act: Art. 12, Art. 26(6) (min. 6 months for high-risk deployer logs)

controls.title: Lawful basis for what the agent does
controls.statement: You have an identified lawful basis or consent for the processing the agent performs, including secondary use the agent creates.
controls.evidence: Records of processing; DPIA where required; consent records.

xw.Other: GDPR Art. 6, Art. 35; HIPAA minimum necessary

domains.name: Identity, Authority & Attribution
domains.purpose: Every agent has its own identity, acts under authority that traces to a human, holds only the privileges its current task needs, and can be shut off individually.
domains.why: The most commonly missing layer, and the one that makes every other control unenforceable when absent. If the agent uses a human's credentials, your logs say a human did it, your revocation kills that human's access, and your least-privilege story is fiction.

controls.title: Distinct identity per agent
controls.statement: You give each agent its own identity. You do not let an agent borrow a human credential, a shared service account, or a long-lived admin credential.
controls.evidence: Identity per agent in the directory or secret store; no shared-credential exceptions outstanding; the agent identity present on an authorization decision record, not only in the directory.

xw.Other: OWASP ASI03, T9; CSA Agentic AI IAM

controls.title: Agent identity lifecycle through the IdP
controls.statement: You create, review, and revoke agent identities through the same identity provider and joiner-mover-leaver process as human identities.
controls.evidence: Provisioning workflow; evidence of a revocation executing end to end.

controls.title: Delegation chain is recorded
controls.statement: For any agent action you can answer: which human authorized it, for what scope, and when that authority started and ended.
controls.evidence: Delegation records or on-behalf-of claims present in logs; a worked example traced from one action record back to the authorizing human — not forward from a grant.

controls.title: Per-action scoping, not per-system
controls.statement: You grant privileges at action granularity: draft but not send, read but not delete. You never hand over a whole business system.
controls.evidence: Scope definitions per connector; a test showing a denied action class.

controls.title: Short-lived, just-in-time credentials
controls.statement: Agents hold credentials scoped to one task and one time window. No standing long-lived static credentials exist.
controls.evidence: Token lifetime configuration; absence of static keys in secret inventory.

controls.title: Audience-bound tokens; no passthrough
controls.statement: Each access token binds to one target resource. This control uses the word token deliberately: the mechanism is OAuth audience binding. A credential presented to one service never travels to another service.
controls.evidence: Token audience validation enabled; architecture review confirming no passthrough path.

xw.Other: MCP authorization spec (RFC 8707 resource indicators; passthrough prohibited)

controls.title: Agent actions distinguishable in logs and SIEM
controls.statement: Agent activity forms a distinct actor class in your security telemetry. You can filter it, alert on it, and separate it from human activity.
controls.evidence: SIEM query returning agent-only activity; actor-type field populated.

controls.title: Granular revocation path
controls.statement: You can revoke one agent, one credential, or one connector without stopping the rest. You have tested this revocation.
controls.evidence: Documented revocation procedure; evidence of a test.

controls.title: Periodic privilege review for agents
controls.statement: The accountable owner reviews agent entitlements at least quarterly, as with human entitlements, and removes accumulated scope.
controls.evidence: Review records with removals actually executed.

domains.name: Ingress Trust & Content Integrity
domains.purpose: Content the agent reads cannot become instructions the agent obeys, and the tools it uses are what they claim to be.
domains.why: Prompt injection and tool poisoning arrive through the normal front door — a ticket description, a web page, a document, an MCP tool description. Normalization and deduplication do not sanitize adversarial content; they launder it into something that looks trusted.

controls.title: Untrusted sources identified and marked
controls.statement: You classify every content source as trusted or untrusted. Untrusted content keeps its marking as it moves through the pipeline.
controls.evidence: Source trust classification; taint or provenance field carried in the context.

controls.title: Injection resistance between content and instruction
controls.statement: A technical boundary stops retrieved or tool-returned content from redirecting the agent goal or authority. A line in the system prompt is not a boundary.
controls.evidence: Architecture description of the boundary; injection test results.

controls.title: Tool, connector and skill approval
controls.statement: You list and approve every tool, plugin, MCP server, connector, and skill an agent can use. Agents cannot add tools at runtime.
controls.evidence: Approved tool register; a blocked attempt to add an unapproved tool.

xw.Other: OWASP ASI04, LLM03; OWASP Agentic Skills Top 10

controls.title: Tool supply-chain integrity
controls.statement: You pin each tool and skill by version or hash and verify its source. You detect when one changes.
controls.evidence: Pinning configuration; integrity verification step in the deployment path.

controls.title: Tool descriptions treated as untrusted
controls.statement: You review tool descriptions at approval and again when they change. The model reads these descriptions and the user does not. A changed description cancels the prior approval.
controls.evidence: Description review record; change-detection mechanism.

xw.Other: MCP spec (annotations untrusted); tool poisoning / rug-pull research; OWASP ASI04

controls.title: Memory and corpus write-path integrity
controls.statement: You control and log every write path into agent memory and retrieval corpora. An agent cannot silently store attacker content for later use.
controls.evidence: Write-path access controls; memory write audit log.

xw.Other: OWASP T1 Memory Poisoning, ASI06, LLM08

controls.title: Output handling before downstream use
controls.statement: You validate, escape, or constrain model output before it executes, renders, or reaches another system. Output never runs as code or as a command.
controls.evidence: Validation layer; test showing an injection payload in output does not execute downstream.

controls.title: Inter-agent messages authenticated and untrusted
controls.statement: In multi-agent systems, agents authenticate their messages to each other. A message from another agent counts as untrusted input, not as a trusted instruction.
controls.evidence: Inter-agent auth mechanism; test showing a spoofed or poisoned message is rejected or contained.

xw.Other: OWASP T12, T13, T14; ASI07; CSA MAESTRO L7

domains.name: Policy Enforcement & Guardrails
domains.purpose: Written policy is turned into an evaluated decision that sits between what the agent wants to do and what it is allowed to do, and cannot be talked out of it.
domains.why: Most 'trust and safety' layers are a checklist of controls with no decision function. A gate needs inputs, a verdict, an unbypassable enforcement point, and a defined behaviour on deny.

controls.title: Policy expressed in evaluable form
controls.statement: The rules that govern agent behaviour exist in a form a machine can evaluate, not only in prose a person can read.
controls.evidence: Policy definitions in code or configuration; mapping from the written policy to the encoded rules.

controls.title: Enforcement point cannot be bypassed
controls.statement: You enforce policy at a chokepoint between decision and action, and the agent cannot route around it. You define three verdicts: allow, deny, and escalate. You connect each verdict to a mechanism that carries it out.
controls.evidence: Architecture showing the enforcement point; test attempting to bypass it; the named mechanism for each verdict, and a test that carries an escalate verdict through to a human decision.

controls.title: Deny is safe and defined
controls.statement: On deny, the system fails closed with defined behaviour. It does not proceed silently, retry with new phrasing, or degrade to an unmonitored path.
controls.evidence: Deny-path specification; log of denials showing what happened next.

controls.title: Ambiguity escalates rather than allows
controls.statement: On an uncertain policy decision, the gate escalates: it holds the action and pages a human. Uncertainty never defaults to permission.
controls.evidence: Escalation rule; escalation volume and resolution records.

controls.title: Prohibited uses enforced technically
controls.statement: Technical controls enforce the prohibited-use list from GOV-03. A policy that people read once is not enforcement.
controls.evidence: Technical control mapped to each prohibited use; test evidence.

controls.title: Output guardrails proportionate to context
controls.statement: You calibrate output guardrails to the audience and the stakes of each use case. One global setting does not fit all uses.
controls.evidence: Guardrail configuration per use case; rationale for the calibration.

controls.title: Policy versioning bound to decisions
controls.statement: Every recorded decision names the policy version that governed it. You judge an old action by the rule in force at the time.
controls.evidence: Policy version identifier present in decision records.

controls.title: Exceptions are time-bound and owned
controls.statement: Each policy exception has a named owner, a written justification, an expiry date, and a review. A permanent exception is a policy change.
controls.evidence: Exception register with expiry dates; evidence of expired exceptions closing.

domains.name: Action Control & Blast Radius
domains.purpose: The agent's ability to cause harm is bounded by construction — by what class of action it may take, how far a mistake can propagate, and how fast you can stop it.
domains.why: This is the layer that has to carry the weight, because the human approval gate empirically does not. Published containment data shows approval rates around 93% and injection success rising sharply under repeated adaptive attempts. Containment must hold when the human clicks Approve.

controls.title: Actions classified by reversibility
controls.statement: You classify every available action as read-only, reversible write, irreversible, or destructive. This class, not the tool name, selects the controls.
controls.evidence: Action inventory with reversibility class per action.

controls.title: Irreversible actions gated or prohibited
controls.statement: Irreversible and destructive actions need explicit human approval, or you remove them from agent reach. Such actions never sit inside the autonomous envelope.
controls.evidence: Configuration showing the gate or the removal; test attempting the action.

controls.title: Isolated execution environment
controls.statement: Agents execute code and use tools inside an isolated environment. The isolation boundary separates them from business systems and from the operator host.
controls.evidence: Sandbox or container configuration; isolation boundary description.

controls.title: Controlled network egress
controls.statement: Agent runtimes have default-deny outbound network access with an explicit allow-list. Egress control limits, but does not remove, exfiltration through approved destinations.
controls.evidence: Egress policy; allow-list with justification per destination.

controls.title: Rate, volume and spend limits with automatic cutoff
controls.statement: Hard limits on invocations, model usage, tool calls, and spend stop the agent automatically. An alert that someone reads later is not a limit.
controls.evidence: Limit configuration; evidence of a cutoff firing.

controls.title: Scope caps per run
controls.statement: Per-run caps bound how much one execution can touch: records changed, messages sent, files changed, recipients addressed. A wrong decision stays small.
controls.evidence: Cap configuration per agent; a run halted by a cap.

xw.Other: CSA Agentic AI Red Teaming (blast-radius minimization)

controls.title: Layered kill switch
controls.statement: You can stop one agent, one connector, one class of write action, or every agent at once. You have tested each layer.
controls.evidence: Kill switch at each layer; test records with time-to-stop measured.

controls.title: Rollback or compensating action
controls.statement: For each reversible write, a defined procedure undoes it, and someone has run that procedure.
controls.evidence: Rollback procedure per action class; test evidence.

controls.title: Autonomy earned incrementally
controls.statement: Agents start gated and earn broader autonomy against pre-stated criteria and performance evidence. Autonomy is a graduation, not a launch setting.
controls.evidence: Promotion criteria; promotion decisions with the supporting evidence.

controls.title: Multi-agent orchestration bounded
controls.statement: Where agents invoke agents, limits bound delegation depth, fan-out, and inherited authority. A sub-agent never gains privileges its caller lacked.
controls.evidence: Orchestration limits in configuration; authority inheritance rules; test of a privilege-escalation attempt via delegation.

xw.Other: OWASP T3, T13, ASI07; CSA MAESTRO

domains.name: Human Oversight & Competence
domains.purpose: The humans in the loop can actually exercise judgment — they have the competence, the information, the authority, and crucially a small enough volume of decisions that their attention still means something.
domains.why: Human oversight is a real control that degrades badly when overused. Approving hundreds of low-consequence prompts trains people to approve the one that matters. Oversight must be rationed to be worth anything.

controls.title: Named, competent, empowered overseers
controls.statement: Named, competent people oversee each agent. They understand its limits and hold the authority to override or stop it without asking permission.
controls.evidence: Assignment records; competence basis; documented authority to stop.

controls.title: Oversight burden is measured
controls.statement: You track how many approvals people receive and the share they approve. A very high approval rate signals a control failure, not health.
controls.evidence: Approval volume and approval-rate metrics over time, reviewed by the accountable owner.

xw.Other: OWASP T10 Overwhelming Human in the Loop

controls.title: Approvals rationed to consequential actions
controls.statement: You require human approval only where it changes the outcome. You remove or automate routine low-consequence confirmations to protect attention for decisions that matter.
controls.evidence: Mapping of which action classes require approval and why; evidence of prompts removed.

controls.title: Approvers get enough to decide
controls.statement: An approval request shows what will happen, to what, why the agent proposes it, and where the agent is uncertain. A bare action name with yes and no is not enough.
controls.evidence: Screenshot or specification of the approval interface.

controls.title: Automation-bias countermeasures
controls.statement: Active measures counter over-trust. Approvers state a reason for consequential approvals, you sample approved actions for later review, and approvers see the agent error record.
controls.evidence: The measure in operation; sampling results.

controls.title: Affected people are informed
controls.statement: When an agent makes or materially shapes a decision about a person, you tell that person an AI system took part.
controls.evidence: Notice text and where it appears in the journey.

xw.Other: CO ADMTA pre-use notice; GDPR Art. 13–14, 22

controls.title: Appeal and human review route
controls.statement: A working route lets a person contest an agent-driven outcome and get human review inside a stated timeframe.
controls.evidence: Documented appeal process; volume and outcome statistics.

xw.Other: CO ADMTA adverse-decision notice (30 days); GDPR Art. 22(3)

controls.title: Disclosure of AI interaction
controls.statement: When a person interacts with an AI system and it would not otherwise be obvious, you tell them.
controls.evidence: The disclosure as it appears to the user.

controls.title: Synthetic content marked
controls.statement: You mark AI-generated or AI-modified content in a machine-readable way and, where the law requires, disclose it to the audience.
controls.evidence: Marking implementation; sample output with the marking present.

xw.EU AI Act: Art. 50(2), 50(4) — applies 2 Aug 2026; existing systems to 2 Dec 2026
xw.Other: C2PA; EU Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-Generated Content (10 Jun 2026)

controls.title: Workforce consultation
controls.statement: Where agents change how people work, how you evaluate them, or how you allocate tasks, you inform workers and their representatives before deployment.
controls.evidence: Consultation records; notification to worker representatives.

controls.title: Override is captured, not punished
controls.statement: You never silently block the ungoverned path: overrides stay possible, always page a human, and convert to a retroactive approval record. You track override rate as system health, never as individual performance. A punished declared override becomes a hidden override.
controls.evidence: Break-glass procedure; one paged override converted to a retroactive record; override-rate metric reviewed by the accountable owner.

domains.name: Observability & Evidence
domains.purpose: You can reconstruct what an agent did, why, on whose authority, and what happened as a result — from a record the agent could not have altered.
domains.why: This is where your original model is strongest: evidence captured at runtime rather than assembled at audit time. The gap to close is integrity — if the actor can write its own record, it is a log, not evidence.

controls.title: Complete action logging
controls.statement: The evidence record captures every tool invocation with the tool, the arguments, the result, and the timestamp. It shows what the agent did, not only that it ran.
controls.evidence: Log sample showing a full tool invocation record.

xw.Other: OWASP T8; OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions (Development status)

controls.title: Attribution is complete
controls.statement: Each entry carries agent identity, the human principal, the session, the policy decision, and the granted scopes. Attribution fails closed: you quarantine unmatched actions for human adjudication and never auto-assign an actor.
controls.evidence: Log schema; a record with all fields populated; the quarantine path for unattributable actions and one adjudicated example.

xw.Other: OWASP T8; CSA Agentic AI IAM

controls.title: Tamper-evident evidence store
controls.statement: The evidence record is append-only or tamper-evident. The agent identity holds no write access to its own evidence path.
controls.evidence: Store configuration; access control showing the agent identity lacks write access to the audit path.

controls.title: Retention meets the longest obligation
controls.statement: You set evidence retention to the longest applicable legal, contractual, or investigative requirement, and you can defend the number.
controls.evidence: Retention configuration and the obligation it maps to.

xw.EU AI Act: Art. 26(6) — at least 6 months for high-risk deployer logs
xw.Other: IL SB 315 / CA SB 53 incident records; CO ADMTA 3-year records

controls.title: End-to-end traceability
controls.statement: One trace links the triggering signal, the retrieved context, the model decision, the policy verdict, the approval, the action, and the outcome.
controls.evidence: A worked trace for a real incident or transaction.

controls.title: Behavioural anomaly detection
controls.statement: You monitor agent behaviour for deviation: unusual volume, novel tool sequences, off-hours activity, and access to new data domains.
controls.evidence: Detection rules; alerts generated and triaged.

xw.Other: MITRE ATLAS agentic techniques (AML.T0080, T0086, T0101)

controls.title: Cost and consumption telemetry
controls.statement: You monitor consumption per agent, so runaway loops and unexpected spend surface early. A cost anomaly can be the first visible symptom of a behavioural one.
controls.evidence: Per-agent cost dashboard; alert thresholds.

controls.title: Evidence is exportable and legible
controls.statement: You can export evidence in a form a regulator, auditor, or customer can use, inside a timeframe you have committed to.
controls.evidence: Export capability; a sample evidence pack.

controls.title: Actor-independent ground truth
controls.statement: At least one telemetry channel records agent effects with zero cooperation from the agent runtime: infrastructure events, database audit logs, or egress logs. You reconcile this channel against the evidence record at least weekly and treat unexplained deltas as findings.
controls.evidence: Sensor configuration; a reconciliation report including at least one investigated delta.

domains.name: Assurance, Evaluation & Red Teaming
domains.purpose: You have evidence the agent behaves acceptably before it goes live and continues to after — including under someone actively trying to make it misbehave.
domains.why: Static, single-attempt testing systematically understates agentic risk. Published evaluation work shows injection success rising from roughly 11% under baseline testing to over 80% under adaptive, multi-attempt attack. If you test once and politely, you will not find what an attacker will.

controls.title: Acceptance criteria defined before launch
controls.statement: You write down what good enough means before the agent goes live, in terms someone could dispute.
controls.evidence: Acceptance criteria document dated before go-live.

controls.title: Task-level evaluation with harm weighting
controls.statement: Evaluation reports per-task outcomes weighted by consequence, not one aggregate pass rate. A deletion failure and a clumsy email are different findings.
controls.evidence: Evaluation report showing per-task results and harm weighting.

controls.title: Adaptive, multi-attempt adversarial testing
controls.statement: Injection and manipulation testing is adaptive and repeated. You report success over N attempts, never a single shot.
controls.evidence: Test methodology and results showing attempt counts.

xw.Other: NIST agent-hijacking evaluations; OWASP AI Testing Guide

controls.title: Red team covers the agentic surface
controls.statement: Red teaming covers tool misuse, privilege escalation, memory and context poisoning, and goal manipulation. Where relevant, it covers inter-agent and rogue-agent scenarios.
controls.evidence: Red team scope mapped to a recognized threat taxonomy; findings and remediation.

xw.Other: OWASP ASI Top 10 (ASI01–ASI10) / threat classes T1–T15; MITRE ATLAS; CSA Agentic AI Red Teaming Guide

controls.title: Fairness and disparate-impact evaluation
controls.statement: Where outputs affect access to opportunity, money, care, or liberty, you measure performance across affected groups, not only in aggregate.
controls.evidence: Disaggregated performance results; the groups tested and why.

xw.Other: US: Title VII, ECOA, FHA; CO ADMTA

controls.title: Model and provider change management
controls.statement: A model version change, a provider default change, or a system prompt change triggers re-evaluation before production. A silent upstream upgrade is a change to your AI system.
controls.evidence: Change process; a re-evaluation record triggered by an upstream change.

controls.title: Model and tool supply-chain assurance
controls.statement: For each model, tool, and dataset you use, you know its origin, licence, security posture, and change terms.
controls.evidence: Supply chain record; provider attestations or assessments.

controls.title: Independent review proportionate to impact
controls.statement: Someone who did not build a high-consequence system reviews it: internal audit, an independent team, or a third party.
controls.evidence: Review report with the reviewer's independence stated.

controls.title: Post-launch drift monitoring
controls.statement: You measure live performance against the acceptance criteria on a schedule. Degradation triggers action, not a note.
controls.evidence: Monitoring dashboard against acceptance thresholds; an example of a triggered response.

controls.title: Dependent controls are tested as a pair
controls.statement: You test controls that depend on each other together, not only one at a time. When one control must invoke another, you name the invocation path and you test it.
controls.evidence: For each dependency, the named invocation path and a test that exercises it end to end; a list of controls that nothing else can reach.

domains.name: Incident Response, Recovery & Retirement
domains.purpose: When an agent does something wrong, you detect it, stop it, undo what can be undone, tell who needs telling, and — when the time comes — retire it cleanly.
domains.why: Agent incidents have a property normal incidents don't: the system may have taken hundreds of small correct-looking actions before the wrong one, so containment and remediation are a search problem, not just a shutdown.

controls.title: AI incidents are in scope of the IR process
controls.statement: Your incident definition covers agent misbehaviour: wrong actions, harmful output, data exposure, and manipulation. The existing incident response process owns these categories.
controls.evidence: IR policy naming AI incident categories.

controls.title: Detection and triage path
controls.statement: A defined path notices and triages agent misbehaviour, with signals from monitoring, from users, and from the people the agent acts upon.
controls.evidence: Detection sources; triage criteria; reporting channel.

controls.title: Containment playbook
controls.statement: A written playbook covers isolating the agent, revoking its credentials, stopping at the right layer, and preserving evidence before it rotates out.
controls.evidence: The playbook; evidence it has been exercised.

xw.Other: NIST SP 800-61 process, AI-specific evidence steps

controls.title: Remediation of actions already taken
controls.statement: You can list everything the agent did in the affected window and reverse or compensate for what needs it.
controls.evidence: Method for enumerating actions in a time window; a worked remediation.

controls.title: Notification obligations mapped in advance
controls.statement: You map who you must tell, and in what timeframe, before the incident: regulator, customer, data subject, insurer, and model provider.
controls.evidence: Notification matrix with timeframes and named contacts.

xw.Other: CA SB 53: Cal OES 15 days / 24h imminent; IL SB 315: 72h / 24h; GDPR Art. 33: 72h

controls.title: Blameless post-incident review
controls.statement: A structured review follows each incident and produces a root cause with named follow-up owners. The review never punishes reporting.
controls.evidence: Post-incident reports with assigned actions and their closure.

controls.title: Clean retirement
controls.statement: Agent retirement follows a defined process: revoke credentials, remove connectors, dispose of memory and derived data per policy, check dependencies, retain evidence.
controls.evidence: Decommissioning checklist; a completed retirement record.

controls.title: Continuity without the agent
controls.statement: If you, an incident, or a provider outage stops the agent, a defined fallback covers its work. You have made the dependence explicit.
controls.evidence: Fallback procedure; the dependency documented in BCP.

domains.name: Learning & Continuous Improvement
domains.purpose: What the system learns in operation changes the system — as specific, owned, tracked artifacts rather than as a resolution to do better.
domains.why: This is the other place your original model is stronger than the published frameworks: it closes the loop to named artifact classes. 'Continuous improvement' is unauditable. 'Seventeen repair items, four monitor tuning changes, two ownership corrections' is auditable.

controls.title: Findings route to named artifact classes
controls.statement: You route operational findings into named, tracked artifact types: remediation items, threshold changes, procedure updates, and ownership corrections. An undifferentiated backlog does not satisfy this control.
controls.evidence: The artifact classes; a report of items by class with closure rates.

controls.title: Control tuning from operational evidence
controls.statement: You update guardrail thresholds, policy rules, and detection logic from operational evidence, and you version each change.
controls.evidence: Change log for guardrails and policies with the triggering evidence.

controls.title: Knowledge artifacts stay current
controls.statement: You version the prompts, procedures, runbooks, and reference material that agents and operators rely on, and update them when found wrong.
controls.evidence: Version history showing updates driven by findings.

controls.title: Ownership corrections feed back to the register
controls.statement: When an incident reveals missing or wrong ownership, you correct the AI register and track the correction to closure.
controls.evidence: Inventory change log tied to findings.

controls.title: Metrics reviewed on a cadence
controls.statement: The accountable owner reviews a defined set of governance metrics on a stated cadence and records the decisions.
controls.evidence: Metric set; review records with decisions.

controls.title: Horizon scanning
controls.statement: A named person tracks changes in regulation, threat technique, and provider capability, and triggers reassessment when any of them moves.
controls.evidence: Named owner; scanning sources; a reassessment triggered by an external change.

controls.title: Sharing beyond the organization
controls.statement: Where sharing is safe and lawful, you share lessons and incident patterns with sector peers and the wider community. You also consume what others share.
controls.evidence: Sharing arrangements; contributions made or received.

xw.Other: MITRE ATLAS case studies; OWASP AI Threat Intelligence Initiative
